title: The Country's Oldest Operating Lighthouse Predates the American Revolution and Still Shines on New York Harbor After More Than 260 Years

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A student and a librarian discuss preserving local historical records for a class project.

script.en: Hi, Professor Martinez suggested I come to you. I'm doing a project on the history of our town's harbor, and I need to find primary sources from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

That sounds like a fascinating topic. We have a special collections room with old maps, shipping records, and some diaries from local merchants. But those materials don't circulate—you'll have to use them here in the library.
That's fine. I'm mostly interested in how the harbor's economy changed over time. Do you have anything about the lighthouses that used to guide ships in?

Actually, we do. We have a ledger from the lighthouse keeper's family, and some photographs from the early twentieth century. But I should warn you—many of the documents are fragile, so you'll need to wear gloves and handle them carefully.
Of course. I've worked with old documents before. Is there a catalog I can search to see what's available?

Yes, our online catalog lists everything, but the descriptions are quite brief. I'd recommend making an appointment with me so I can pull the most relevant items for you. That way you won't waste time.
That would be great. I'm particularly curious about how the lighthouse keepers lived—their daily routines, the challenges they faced.

The ledger should help with that. It records weather conditions, ship arrivals, and even some personal notes. It's a rare glimpse into their lives. Just keep in mind that the handwriting can be difficult to read.
I'll manage. I'm also wondering if there are any oral histories from people whose families worked at the lighthouse.

We have a few recorded interviews from the 1970s with descendants of lighthouse keepers. They're on cassette tapes, though, so you'd need to use our listening station. I can set that up for you when you come in.
Perfect. So should I email you to schedule a time?
Yes, send me a message with your project details and a few possible times. I'll reserve the materials and have them ready. And bring a notebook—you won't be able to use a pen near the documents.

script.en: Lighthouses have long captured the public imagination, but their role in modern navigation has changed dramatically over the past century. For centuries, these coastal beacons served as essential guides for ships navigating treacherous waters, warning sailors of hidden reefs and rocky shorelines. Keepers maintained the lights through violent storms and long periods of isolation, often living on remote sites for years at a time. However, the twentieth century brought a series of technologies that gradually reduced their importance in everyday maritime operations. Radio communication allowed ships to determine their position and receive warnings without relying on visual signals from the shore. Radar enabled vessels to detect hazards even in fog or darkness, greatly improving safety at sea. Later, the development of satellite-based positioning systems, originally designed for military use, made precise navigation available to all. As a result, the number of operational lighthouses has declined steadily. Today, only about half of the roughly 800 lighthouses standing in the United States remain active. Many have been abandoned or transferred to local organizations for preservation. Some have become museums or tourist attractions, drawing visitors interested in maritime history, and yet the transition has not been without controversy. Preservationists argue that these structures are irreplaceable cultural landmarks that tell the story of the nation's maritime past. They point out that once a lighthouse is lost to neglect or erosion, it cannot be rebuilt. Others emphasize the high cost of maintenance and question whether public funds should be spent on structures no longer needed for navigation. Despite the debate, many communities have rallied to save their local lighthouses, raising money and organizing volunteer efforts. The story of lighthouses thus reflects a broader question: how should society balance the preservation of historical heritage against the demands of modern technology and limited resources?

sections.title: The Lighthouse That Helped Build a Nation
sections.passage: Until the 20th century, the only safe maritime route into New York Harbor wound between shallow shoals, with a particularly dangerous point where the shipping lane curved around the northern tip of the Sandy Hook peninsula. After devastating shipwrecks in 1761, New York's merchants petitioned the Colonial Assembly to build a navigational aid. Using £750 raised by lottery, the Assembly purchased four acres near the peninsula's tip. On June 11, 1764, the fifth lighthouse in the Colonies was lit atop a solid, tapered octagon of whitewashed rubblestone, 103 feet high. When the Revolutionary War began, rebel troops tried to dismantle the lantern to keep British ships from navigating into the harbor. Their efforts included an April 1776 escapade in which a New Jersey troupe trapped British soldiers in the upper room by removing the lower stairs. But Sandy Hook soon fell under British control, and several other attacks failed to destroy the structure or wrest it from the royalists. The walls, more than six feet thick at the base, were simply too strong. When the British finally withdrew from their last American strongholds, they blasted and burned the Boston Light in 1776 and the Beavertail Light in Rhode Island in 1779, two of the Colonies' oldest beacons. By the end of the century, two other lighthouses predating Sandy Hook had succumbed to age, fire and battering seas. Today, Sandy Hook is the oldest continuously operational lighthouse in the United States and a remarkably rich emblem for a pivotal moment in American statecraft. Before the 1789 Lighthouse Act, which made the country's 12 surviving lighthouses national property, the federal state was merely a state of mind, writes Allen S. Miller, a longtime intelligence and risk-management analyst. Predating the act that formally created the Department of the Treasury and signed the same day as the act creating the Department of War, the Lighthouse Act turned those isolated beacons into a pointillist network of federal infrastructure, unifying a fledgling maritime economy and helping invent a durable and coherent United States. The Sandy Hook tower also served as a model for the first lighthouses the U.S. built after independence, through the extraordinary surge in construction in the 19th century. In 1820, there were 55 lighthouses in the United States; by 1910, nearly 1,400. These beacons served a booming maritime shipping economy. Between 1834 and 1860 alone, the number of vessels entering New York Harbor from the Atlantic doubled—and because cargo ships were getting bigger and more efficient, the estimated collective weight of their cargo increased fourfold. But there were early signs that the light wouldn't burn forever: as early as the Civil War, drifting sand deposits extended the coastline and eroded the lighthouse's commercial significance. Where in 1764 the lighthouse stood just 500 feet from the tip of the peninsula, by 1864 the distance had increased to 4,000 feet. Now it's nearly a mile and a half. Technological transformations in the 20th century, like radio, radar and the position-fixing system known as LORAN-C, gradually pushed lighthouse keepers, and eventually lighthouses themselves, into obsolescence.

long_sentences.en: His last words, it’s said, were: “Mind the lights, Katie.” According to the U.S. Coast Guard, Walker “not only kept the light burning but by her own account may have saved as many as 50 people.” Technological transformations in the 20th century, like radio, radar and the position-fixing system known as LORAN-C (plus earlier inventions like electric batteries and lanterns), gradually pushed lighthouse keepers, and eventually lighthouses themselves, into obsolescence.

At one particularly treacherous point, the shipping lane bent around the northern tip of the Sandy Hook peninsula, which the English politician Thomas Pownall described in 1755 as “a neck of low sandy hills covered with cedars and holly, ending in a low sandy point.” After a devastating series of shipwrecks in 1761, New York’s merchants petitioned the Colonial Assembly to build a navigational aid.

Predating the act that formally created the Department of Treasury, and signed the same day as the act creating the Department of War, the Lighthouse Act turned those isolated beacons into a pointillist network of federal infrastructure, unifying a fledgling maritime economy and, in the process, helping invent a durable and coherent United States.
